(CNN) -- Remember the worst job you ever had? You know, back when there were jobs to be had? Jesse Eisenberg tries to strike up a relationship with Kristen Stewart in "Adventureland." For writer-director Greg Mottola, it was the summer he spent on hiatus between college and the real world, working as a carny at the local carnival. He's turned the experience into the basis for the wonderful "Adventureland." Handing out stuffed animals to the lucky customer whose tin horse romps home in first place -- this is not how James (Jesse Eisenberg from "The Squid and the Whale") would choose to see himself. The paycheck is dismal, but undeniably commensurate with (as a character puts it) "the work of pathetic, lazy morons," which is what it comes down to. Most jobs have their compensations, though. At Adventureland, for James, the biggest benefit comes in the form of Em (Kristen Stewart), another recent grad with plans to move to New York in the fall, and who isn't entirely disdainful of his company. Last time out of the gate Mottola enjoyed a hit with the spectacularly lewd "Superbad," an angle that Miramax Films is understandably keen to play up in the marketing this time around. At first glance the cap seems to fit. James' sexual experience -- or rather the lack of it -- is a defining element in the story. "Adventureland" comes with the usual farcical peccadilloes of teen comedy -- barf gags, car wrecks and inopportune erections -- as well as several familiar supporting players from the Judd Apatow stable. Bill Hader and Kristen Wiig are engagingly upbeat as the mutually besotted park managers, and Martin Starr (from "Freaks and Geeks") is James' cerebral, pipe-smoking buddy, Joel. (Mottola directed a couple of episodes of Apatow's short-lived Fox series "Undeclared.") There's also an extended cameo from Ryan Reynolds, an actor whose faintly supercilious good looks have graced innumerable dumb slacker comedies, including "Van Wilder," "Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle" and "Waiting." Yet, after an initial flurry of gross guffaws, the movie edges toward something rather different: a nuanced, sensitive coming-of-age story that finds its heart in post-adolescent romantic turmoil. Obviously adept with actors, Mottola respects his characters too much to let first impressions stick. The relationships in "Adventureland" are much richer, and stickier, for it. The understanding that James arrives at with his father (Jack Gilpin), for example, is delineated in just a handful of looks and glances between them, but it's enough to imply the older man's resignation at his fate, and his appreciation for James' tacit sympathy. It's in moments like these (and there are a number of them) that we're reminded Mottola made a fine indie movie, "The Daytrippers," more than a decade ago now, another sharp and tender comic distillation of family bonds and fractures. Blessed with comical seriousness, Eisenberg is like a young Woody Allen: fretful, intelligent, naive and deluded. And like Allen, he seems to enjoy more than his fair share of luck with the opposite sex. Still, "Adventureland" makes more effort than "Superbad" -- not that hard admittedly -- to develop a character for Stewart. Looking wan and pensive (the "Twilight" star always looks in need of a good night's sleep), Stewart as Em gives the impression she's living life more acutely than the others. She seems to have more on the line. Set in the mid-'80s, the film suggests the period unobtrusively, but predominantly through pop music. Lou Reed provides sweet relief to repeated bursts of Falco's "Rock Me Amadeus." Yes, in retrospect, that's exactly what being young in 1987 was like. A mature movie about immature young people, "Adventureland" may be too muted to succeed in today's marketplace, too sensitive for its own good. Like an anxious parent, a critic can only send it on its way and hope the world treats it well. "Adventureland" is rated R and runs 107 minutes. For Entertainment Weekly's take, click here.

(CNN) -- Do you remember the worst job you ever held? Back when jobs, of course, were still there to be had? For writer-director Greg Mottola, that dubious distinction belongs to the summer he spent between college and the demands of the real world, working as a carny at his local amusement park. He has since transformed that experience into the foundation for the thoroughly enjoyable "Adventureland."

Handing out stuffed animals to whichever lucky customer's tin horse happens to romp home first is hardly how James (Jesse Eisenberg, of "The Squid and the Whale") would choose to envision his future. The pay is dismal, though undeniably fitting for what one character bluntly describes as "the work of pathetic, lazy morons" — which, in truth, is precisely what it amounts to.

Most jobs, however, offer some form of compensation. For James, the greatest reward at Adventureland comes in the form of Em (Kristen Stewart), a fellow recent graduate with plans to relocate to New York come autumn, who proves not entirely immune to his company.

Mottola's previous outing yielded the gloriously raunchy hit "Superbad," an association Miramax Films is understandably eager to emphasize in its marketing of this new film. At first glance, the comparison seems apt: James' sexual inexperience — or rather, his conspicuous lack thereof — forms a defining thread of the narrative. "Adventureland" delivers the familiar comic trappings of teen cinema — vomit gags, car crashes, and ill-timed erections — alongside several recognizable faces from the Judd Apatow ensemble. Bill Hader and Kristen Wiig bring buoyant charm to their roles as the mutually smitten park managers, while Martin Starr (of "Freaks and Geeks") plays James' pipe-smoking, cerebral confidant, Joel. (Mottola, notably, directed several episodes of Apatow's short-lived Fox series "Undeclared.") The film also features an extended cameo from Ryan Reynolds, whose faintly self-satisfied good looks have graced countless slacker comedies, among them "Van Wilder," "Harold & Kumar Go to White Castle," and "Waiting."

Yet after its initial flourish of crude laughs, the film gradually reveals itself to be something altogether different: a nuanced, tender coming-of-age story rooted in the emotional turbulence of post-adolescent romance. Clearly skilled in his direction of actors, Mottola holds his characters in too much regard to let first impressions define them. As a result, the relationships within "Adventureland" emerge as far richer — and far more complicated — than they might first appear.

The quiet understanding James reaches with his father (Jack Gilpin), for instance, is conveyed through little more than a handful of glances exchanged between them — yet it is enough to suggest the older man's weary acceptance of his circumstances, along with his gratitude for his son's unspoken empathy. It is in moments such as these — and there are several — that one is reminded Mottola once crafted a fine independent film, "The Daytrippers," more than a decade ago: another sharp, tender meditation on the bonds and fractures within family.

Endowed with a kind of comic gravity, Eisenberg channels something of a young Woody Allen — anxious, intelligent, naive, and self-deluding. And like Allen, he appears to enjoy more than his fair share of good fortune with women. Still, "Adventureland" makes a noticeably greater effort than "Superbad" — admittedly not a high bar — to give Stewart's character genuine depth. Looking wan and pensive, as though perpetually in need of a good night's sleep (a quality familiar to fans of her "Twilight" persona), Stewart's Em conveys the sense of someone living life with greater intensity than those around her — someone with more at stake.

Set in the mid-1980s, the film evokes its era with a light touch, relying largely on its soundtrack to do so. Lou Reed offers welcome respite amid repeated bursts of Falco's "Rock Me Amadeus" — and yes, in hindsight, that does seem to capture something essential about being young in 1987.

A mature film about immature people, "Adventureland" may prove too understated for today's marketplace, too delicate for its own good. Like an anxious parent watching a child venture into the world, a critic can only send it forth and hope it is met with the reception it deserves.

"Adventureland" is rated R and runs 107 minutes. For Entertainment Weekly's take, click here.

Writer-director Greg Mottola mined his own past for inspiration when crafting "Adventureland," drawing on a summer he once spent working at a Pittsburgh-area amusement park to create a story that feels lived-in and authentic rather than manufactured for laughs. The film follows James Brennan (Jesse Eisenberg), a bookish, idealistic college graduate whose dreams of a summer backpacking through Europe—and later, graduate school in New York—are dashed when his father's financial troubles leave him broke and stranded at home. Given Mottola's previous directorial success with "Superbad"—a raucous, crude, and hugely popular teen comedy—and the presence of several actors associated with Judd Apatow's comedic universe (including Bill Hader and Kristen Wiig in supporting roles), "Adventureland" was marketed to audiences expecting another gross-out romp filled with over-the-top gags and youthful hijinks. However, the film reveals itself to be something markedly different: a wistful, semi-autobiographical reflection on the awkwardness, disappointment, and unexpected beauty of the transition into adulthood. While it retains some of the recognizable trappings of the teen comedy genre—first loves, workplace antics, and the search for identity—"Adventureland" distinguishes itself through its restraint, its melancholic undertones, and its willingness to let its characters sit with uncertainty rather than resolving every conflict with a punchline.

# The Things We Choose to Remember

CNN flickers across the screen in the background—another headline, another crisis, another day of information washing over us like waves against a shore. You sit there, half-listening, half-lost in thought, and wonder how much of it you'll actually remember tomorrow.

Memory is a strange curator. It doesn't preserve everything equally. The news cycle moves so fast now that stories which dominated headlines just months ago have already faded into a hazy blur, replaced by newer urgencies. CNN and outlets like it compete for our attention in an endless stream, but our minds simply cannot hold onto it all.

What you choose to remember says something about who you are. Perhaps it's not the breaking news alerts or the pundits' analysis that stays with you, but a single image, a particular phrase, or the way a story made you feel in that moment. Maybe you remember exactly where you were sitting when you heard certain news, even if the details of the event itself have grown fuzzy with time.

There's something worth considering in this: in an age of constant information flow, what deserves to be remembered? Not everything that flashes across CNN's chyron will matter in a year, or even a week. But some moments—the ones that shift how you see the world, that make you pause and reconsider—those are the ones worth holding onto.

Perhaps the real skill isn't consuming more information, but learning what to let go of, and what to carry forward. You get to decide, ultimately, what earns a permanent place in your memory and what simply passes through, like so much noise in an increasingly loud world.

# 'Adventureland' Trades Raunch for Something More Real

There's a moment in "Adventureland" where the carefully constructed expectations set by its marketing come crashing down—in the best possible way. Director Greg Mottola, fresh off the raunchy triumph of "Superbad," has delivered something far more wistful and melancholic than audiences might expect, and the film is all the better for it.

Set in the summer of 1987, "Adventureland" follows James Brennan (Jesse Eisenberg), a recent college graduate whose plans for a European backpacking trip evaporate when his family's finances take a hit. Instead, he finds himself working at a shabby Pittsburgh amusement park, running rigged games and dealing with a colorful cast of coworkers who become his unlikely summer family.

## A Cast That Finds the Human Moments

Eisenberg, still a few years from his career-defining turn in "The Social Network," brings a nervy, bookish sincerity to James that feels lived-in rather than performed. He's matched beautifully by Kristen Stewart, in a pre-"Twilight" role that reminds us she was once celebrated for exactly this kind of naturalistic, guarded vulnerability. As Em, a girl carrying more emotional baggage than she lets on, Stewart delivers what may still be one of her most textured performances.

The supporting cast is where Mottola's affection for his characters truly shines. Ryan Reynolds finds unexpected shading in a role that could have been a one-note joke—the aging park employee still clinging to rock-star fantasies. Bill Hader and Kristen Wiig, as the park's owners, provide comic relief without tipping into caricature, while Martin Starr's deadpan intellectual snob is a scene-stealing delight.

## Tone: Nostalgic, Not Nostalgic-for-Nostalgia's-Sake

What separates "Adventureland" from lesser coming-of-age fare is its refusal to romanticize its era or its characters. The film is soaked in specific, unglamorous period detail—the amusement park itself is tackier than charming, the music choices feel authentic rather than curated for maximum needle-drop impact, and the emotional stakes feel genuinely uncertain rather than predetermined by genre convention.

Mottola isn't interested in easy laughs here so much as the particular ache of being twenty-two and directionless, of loving someone who might not be ready to love you back, of realizing your parents are flawed and human. There's humor throughout, but it emerges organically from character rather than being engineered for maximum crowd response.

## The "Superbad" Comparison—And Why It's Misleading

Here's where marketing has done "Adventureland" a disservice: audiences expecting "Superbad 2.0" are likely to leave confused or disappointed. Where "Superbad" was propulsive, profane, and built around big comic set pieces, "Adventureland" is patient, melancholic, and more interested in quiet emotional truths than in escalating chaos.

This isn't a knock on either film—they're simply different animals. "Superbad" captured a specific kind of male adolescent anxiety through broad comedy; "Adventureland" is interested in something closer to genuine heartbreak and the particular limbo of post-college uncertainty. Mottola deserves credit for not simply repeating himself, even if it means some audiences will feel misled by a marketing campaign eager to capitalize on his previous hit.

## The Verdict

"Adventureland" won't deliver the gut-busting, quotable moments of "Superbad," and viewers should adjust their expectations accordingly. What it offers instead is something quieter and, in many ways, more resonant: a coming-of-age story that trusts its characters' emotional complexity over cheap laughs, anchored by performances—particularly from Eisenberg and Stewart—that linger well after the credits roll.

It's the kind of film that might not fully register on first viewing, but rewards patience with an authenticity that too many nostalgia-soaked coming-of-age films never bother to earn.

**Rating: 3.5 out of 4 stars**

# Adventureland: A Critical Review

Greg Mottola's 2009 film arrived with a marketing campaign that misleadingly positioned it as a spiritual successor to *Superbad*, which Mottola had directed two years prior. Audiences expecting broad raunch-com beats instead found something quieter, more melancholic, and considerably more interested in emotional truth than punchlines. This tonal bait-and-switch likely hurt the film commercially, but viewed on its own terms, *Adventureland* is a thoughtful, if uneven, coming-of-age drama that uses comedy as a delivery mechanism for something more wistful.

## The Shift in Register

The film's greatest strength—and occasional weakness—is its refusal to commit fully to either comedic or dramatic registers. Mottola sets up the amusement park as a natural comedic sandbox: dead-end jobs, rigged games, eccentric coworkers, and Bill Hader and Kristen Wiig doing reliably funny work as the park's managers. But the film consistently pulls back from broad comedy in favor of something quieter and sadder.

Jesse Eisenberg's James Brennan, fresh out of college with vague literary ambitions and no money for grad school, functions as an early prototype for the anxious, hyper-verbal persona Eisenberg would later refine. His romance with Kristen Stewart's Em is the emotional core of the film, and it's here that Mottola's dramatic instincts are strongest—the relationship is built on genuine loneliness and class friction rather than genre convention. Em's affair with Ryan Reynolds' married maintenance man Mike Connell adds a layer of quiet desperation that the film handles with more nuance than its trailer ever suggested.

## Where It Falters

The tonal shift isn't always graceful. Secondary comic characters—particularly Martin Starr's dry, cigarette-smoking intellectual Joel—sometimes feel like they've wandered in from a different, funnier movie, creating a slight structural imbalance. The film also occasionally succumbs to nostalgia-signaling that feels more like production design than lived experience; the 1987 setting is rendered through needle drops and period detail that sometimes substitute for texture rather than earning it.

Reynolds' character, meanwhile, exists in a strange narrative purgatory—meant to represent a cautionary adult failure-state for James, but never quite given enough interiority to be more than a plot device.

## What Works

Where the film succeeds is in its unforced observation of a particular kind of purgatorial summer—the one between the end of formal education and the uncertain beginning of adult life. Mottola, drawing on his own biography, understands the specific humiliation of applying oneself to a job that requires no application at all, and the strange intimacy that forms between people whose only real connection is shared boredom.

The comedy, when it does land, serves this melancholy rather than undercutting it. Hader and Wiig's shtick is broad, but it's contrasted against James and Em's more subdued rapport in a way that suggests two different registers of coping with disappointment—one loud, one quiet.

## Verdict

*Adventureland* is best understood not as a comedy with dramatic detours, but as a drama that uses comedic infrastructure—familiar character types, a workplace setting, era-appropriate signifiers—to tell a fairly unsentimental story about arrested ambition and first heartbreak. It's a lesser film than *Superbad* in terms of craft consistency, but a more emotionally ambitious one. Mottola's willingness to let the comedy recede in service of feeling marks this as a transitional work—one that points toward the more character-driven instincts he'd bring to television work later in his career, even if the film itself doesn't always know exactly what it wants to be.

**Rating: 3/5** — A film more interesting for its ambition and specificity than fully successful in execution, but worth watching for Stewart and Eisenberg's chemistry and Mottola's clear affection for a very particular kind of purgatorial summer.

Greg Mottola's *Adventureland* (2009) arrived in theaters carrying the weight of expectations it never quite asked for. Marketed alongside the wave of raunchy comedies that had defined late-2000s cinema, the film found itself unfairly compared to Mottola's previous directorial effort, *Superbad*, and the broader Apatow comedy universe that dominated the era. # "Adventureland": A Bittersweet Ride Through Lost Summers

*Film Review*

There's a particular kind of ache that comes with remembering the summer between who you were and who you're about to become. Greg Mottola's "Adventureland" captures that feeling with a precision that feels less like filmmaking and more like memory itself—hazy around the edges, sharper than expected at the center.

**Setting the Scene**

Mottola, working from his own experiences running games at a Pittsburgh amusement park in the 1980s, resists the temptation to turn the decade into caricature. There are no neon leg warmers or excessive mullets played for cheap laughs. Instead, the production design leans into a lived-in shabbiness: the flickering carnival lights, the grease-stained employee break room, the particular indignity of a polyester park uniform. Adventureland itself—the fictional amusement park that gives the film its title—becomes a purgatory of sorts, a liminal space where college-bound kids kill time before their real lives begin.

The film's late-80s setting isn't just backdrop; it's thematic scaffolding. This is a pre-internet, pre-cell phone world where boredom breeds intimacy, where you actually have to *talk* to people because there's nothing else to do. That analog loneliness gives the romance at the film's center room to breathe.

**The Soundtrack as Emotional GPS**

Few films use music as effectively as "Adventureland" does to mark time and mood. The soundtrack—stacked with Falco's "Rock Me Amadeus," Lou Reed's melancholic drift, and the omnipresent, park-mandated repetition of certain painfully catchy pop songs—does double duty. It's authentic to the era without feeling like a greatest-hits playlist assembled by committee. There's a running gag involving a single detestable song blaring on loop that becomes a clever metaphor for the characters' entrapment, both literal and existential.

**Performances That Transcend the Genre**

Jesse Eisenberg, in the years before he'd become synonymous with rapid-fire cynicism, plays James with a soft, stammering earnestness that feels refreshingly unpolished. He's awkward without being a punchline—a college graduate forced back into his parents' orbit, uncertain and a little sad in a way that never tips into self-pity.

Stewart's performance is all internal weather; you can see her recalculating, deciding how much of herself to reveal, in real time. The chemistry between her and Eisenberg feels unforced—two people circling each other with the particular hesitance of those who've been hurt before and know better than to trust happiness easily.

Martin Starr, as the erudite, Slavic-lit-quoting Joel, quietly steals scenes with a performance that suggests entire unspoken novels of disappointment and hope.

**The Verdict**

"Adventureland" doesn't reinvent the coming-of-age wheel, but it turns it with unusual tenderness. # Adventureland: A Coming-of-Age Story Sold as Something It's Not

When *Adventureland* hit theaters in 2009, its marketing campaign told audiences one story while the film itself told a completely different one. Trailers packed with quick cuts, wisecracks, and the promise of raucous, *Superbad*-style hijinks positioned Greg Mottola's follow-up to that 2007 hit as another entry in the raunchy comedy canon. What audiences actually got was something far more delicate, melancholic, and emotionally honest—a mismatch that likely hurt the film's box office performance but shouldn't diminish its reputation as one of the more quietly affecting coming-of-age films of its era.

## The Bait-and-Switch

It's easy to understand the studio's reasoning. Mottola had just delivered a massive hit with *Superbad*, and star Jesse Eisenberg was riding the same indie-comedy wave that made Michael Cera a household name. Kristen Stewart, meanwhile, was fresh off *Twilight*, bringing in an entirely different audience expecting a specific brand of brooding romance. The marketing tried to have it both ways—selling laughs to comedy fans and chemistry to Twihards—while burying what the film actually is: a wistful, autobiographical-feeling portrait of post-college aimlessness, first love, and the particular sadness of realizing your life hasn't turned out the way you planned.

## What the Film Actually Is

Set in 1987, *Adventureland* follows James (Eisenberg), a recent college graduate whose plans for a European backpacking trip evaporate when his father's demotion leaves the family without money. Forced to take a humiliating summer job running games at a rundown amusement park, James finds himself adrift among a cast of similarly stuck twenty-somethings, including Stewart's Em, a girl carrying her own quiet burden of grief and a complicated affair with the park's married maintenance man (Ryan Reynolds, cast wonderfully against type).

The comedy here is real, but it's observational and character-based rather than gag-driven. There's no vomit, no gross-out set pieces, no quotable one-liners designed for trailer cuts. Instead, there's the specific comedy of humiliation—James getting knocked out cold by a stuffed panda, the Sisyphean torment of a game rigged so no one can ever win. It's funny because it's true, not because it's engineered to be quotable.

## The Emotional Core

What Mottola is really interested in is the specific texture of feeling stuck—the way early adulthood can feel like a holding pattern, full of jobs you're overqualified and underqualified for simultaneously, relationships that feel enormous precisely because your world has temporarily shrunk to the size of a theme park parking lot. Eisenberg, playing a gentler variation on his usual anxious-intellectual persona, makes James's sexual and emotional inexperience feel poignant rather than pathetic. Stewart, in one of her best pre-*Twilight*-backlash performances, gives Em a wounded intelligence that never tips into melodrama.

The film's best scenes are its quietest ones: James and Em bonding over cigarettes and shared cultural references, an aching moment involving a Lou Reed song, the slow-building revelation of why Em is drawn to a man who will never truly choose her. This is a film more interested in silences and hesitations than punchlines.

## The Cost of Misleading Marketing

The disconnect between advertising and content created a strange critical and commercial fate for *Adventureland*. Audiences expecting broad laughs left confused or disappointed; audiences who might have embraced its quieter charms never showed up because the marketing gave them no reason to. It's a familiar Hollywood problem—studios reluctant to sell "small" or "sad" films as such—but it's particularly frustrating here because the film doesn't need the disguise. It's genuinely funny in the way real life is funny, and genuinely moving in ways that don't require exaggeration.

## Final Verdict

Divorced from its misleading marketing, *Adventureland* reveals itself as a low-key gem—a film more interested in the ache of arrested development than the theatrics of gross-out comedy. It shares more DNA with Cameron Crowe's *Say Anything* or Mottola's own underappreciated eye for period specificity than with the Apatow comedies it was sold alongside. Watching it now, years removed from its marketing missteps, it's easier to appreciate what Mottola actually built: not a comedy with heart, but a drama with jokes, filled with the particular sadness and sweetness of realizing that growing up rarely goes according to plan.

**Grade: B+**
